regulation_summaries.title: SEC-Style Summary: Public Company Periodic Disclosure (Fictional Example)
regulation_summaries.content:
This is a fictional, simplified summary created for demo purposes, not real SEC rule text.

                        General concept: Public companies are generally expected to file periodic
                        reports (such as annual and quarterly reports) that disclose their financial
                        condition, results of operations, and material events that could affect an
                        investor's decision to buy, hold, or sell the company's securities.

                        Illustrative example: 'Meridian Capital Partners' (a fictional company used
                        for this example) would be expected to file an annual report summarizing its
                        fiscal year results and a quarterly report each quarter, plus a current report
                        promptly after any material event such as a leadership change or major
                        acquisition.

regulation_summaries.title: FINRA-Style Summary: Suitability Obligation (Fictional Example)
regulation_summaries.content:
This is a fictional, simplified summary created for demo purposes, not real
                        FINRA rule text.

                        General concept: A broker-dealer's recommendation to a customer is generally
                        expected to be suitable given the customer's investment profile, including
                        factors such as age, financial situation, investment experience, time horizon,
                        liquidity needs, and risk tolerance.

                        Illustrative example: A representative at 'Northbridge Advisory Group' (a
                        fictional firm used for this example) recommending a complex derivatives
                        strategy to a customer would generally be expected to first assess whether
                        that customer's investment profile supports that level of risk.

regulation_summaries.title: SEC-Style Summary: Insider Trading / Material Nonpublic Information (Fictional Example)
regulation_summaries.content:
This is a fictional, simplified summary created for demo purposes, not real
                        SEC rule text.

                        General concept: Trading a company's securities while in possession of
                        material information that has not been made public, or passing that
                        information to others who trade on it, is generally prohibited.

                        Illustrative example: An employee of fictional company 'Solara Biotech Inc.'
                        (a fictional company used for this example) who learns of an unannounced
                        clinical trial result would generally be expected to refrain from trading
                        Solara shares, or tipping others, until the information is publicly disclosed.

regulation_summaries.title: OCC-Style Summary: Bank Capital Adequacy (Fictional Example)
regulation_summaries.content:
This is a fictional, simplified summary created for demo purposes, not real
                        OCC rule text.

                        General concept: National banks are generally expected to maintain capital
                        reserves proportionate to their risk-weighted assets, to remain resilient
                        under financial stress.

                        Illustrative example: Fictional 'Cascade National Bank' (a fictional bank
                        used for this example) would be expected to periodically report its capital
                        ratios to its regulator and maintain them above the applicable regulatory
                        minimums.

regulation_summaries.title: FinCEN-Style Summary: Suspicious Activity Reporting (Fictional Example)
regulation_summaries.content:
This is a fictional, simplified summary created for demo purposes, not real
                        FinCEN rule text.

                        General concept: Financial institutions are generally expected to monitor
                        customer transactions and file a suspicious activity report (SAR) when a
                        transaction pattern appears potentially related to money laundering or other
                        financial crime, regardless of whether wrongdoing is confirmed.

                        Illustrative example: If a fictional customer at 'Northbridge Advisory Group'
                        (a fictional firm used for this example) made a series of transfers just
                        below a reporting threshold, that pattern might be flagged for internal
                        review under an AML monitoring program.
